2.1: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: Sāṃkhya is mainly knowledge (SK 64); kriyā-yoga is Yoga’s practical bridge to it. Veda: all three come from the Upaniṣads — Taittirīya Up. 3.2 ‘know Brahman by tapas’; 1.9 repeats ‘study and teaching (svādhyāya-pravacana)’ after every virtue; Śvetāśvatara Up. 6.18 — ‘I go for refuge to that God.’ Meaning: austerity, study and surrender are the Vedic disciplines, condensed.
2.2: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: the kleśas are SK 47–48’s five forms of error (viparyaya); thinning them prepares buddhi for discrimination (SK 37). Veda: Muṇḍaka Up. 3.1.5 — ‘this Self is gained by truth, tapas, right knowledge and constant brahmacarya’. Meaning: discipline does not produce liberation; it clears the ground.
2.3: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 48 names five kinds of error — tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra, andhatāmisra. Vyāsa and the Sāṃkhya commentators equate them one-to-one with these five: ignorance, I-am-ness, attraction, aversion, clinging to life. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.2.5 — the deluded, ‘thinking themselves wise’, go round and round. Meaning: the two schools name the same five knots.
2.4: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: avidyā is the field because SK 44 makes error (viparyaya) the cause of bondage; the other kleśas grow from it. Veda: Īśa Up. 9 — ‘into blind darkness enter those who worship ignorance’; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 4.4.5 — desire, resolve and action follow one another. Meaning: dormant or active, every affliction is ignorance in some stage of growth.
2.5: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 64’s insight — ‘I am not, nothing is mine, no I’ — is the exact reversal of this fourfold mistake. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 2.1.2 — ‘the childish follow outward desires … the wise, knowing immortality, do not seek the permanent among things impermanent.’ Meaning: ignorance is a confusion of labels — permanent for passing, Self for not-Self.
2.6: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: asmitā is ahaṃkāra (SK 24, ‘self-arrogation’), and its effect is SK 20 — the instrument seems to be the seer. Veda: Gītā 3.27 — ‘actions are done by the guṇas of prakṛti; one deluded by ahaṃkāra thinks “I am the doer.”’ Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 1.4.10 shows the corrected form: ‘I am Brahman.’ Meaning: the trouble is not ‘I’, but which thing gets called ‘I’.
2.7: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 45 — from attachment (rāga) comes rebirth. Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 4.4.5 — ‘as is his desire, so is his will; as is his will, so his action; as his action, so he becomes.’ Gītā 2.62 traces the same chain from dwelling on objects. Meaning: attraction is memory of pleasure leaning forward.
2.8: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: aversion is SK 48’s tāmisra, ‘gloom’. Veda: Īśa Up. 6 — ‘one who sees all beings in the Self … feels no aversion (na vijugupsate)’. Meaning: aversion is memory of pain leaning away; seeing the Self in others dissolves it.
2.9: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: abhiniveśa is andhatāmisra, ‘blind gloom’ (SK 48); SK 55 locates suffering in decay and death. Veda: Ṛgveda 7.59.12 — ‘release me from death, as a cucumber from its stalk’; Atharvaveda 10.8.44 — knowing the desireless, ageless Self ‘one does not fear death’. Meaning: fear of death runs even in the learned, until the deathless is known.
2.10: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: ‘pratiprasava’, flowing back to source, is the evolution of SK 22 run in reverse — effects dissolving into their causes. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.3.13 — merge speech into mind, mind into intellect, intellect into the great self, that into the peaceful Self. Meaning: subtle seeds are not fought; they are dissolved upstream.
2.11: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: the active forms are buddhi’s vṛttis (SK 23); meditation weakens them. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.2.12 — ‘by the yoga of the inner self (adhyātma-yoga), the wise one leaves joy and sorrow behind.’ Meaning: the Upaniṣad’s own name for this method is adhyātma-yoga.
2.12: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 40–42 — the subtle body carries dispositions from life to life; this is that storehouse. Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 4.4.5 — ‘one becomes good by good action, bad by bad’; Chāndogya Up. 3.14.1 — ‘as one’s resolve is in this world, so one becomes on departing.’ Meaning: karma is stored intention waiting for its season.
2.13: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 44 — virtue leads upward, vice downward; SK 53 lists the kinds of birth. Veda: Chāndogya Up. 5.10.7 — ‘those of pleasant conduct quickly enter a pleasant womb’; Kaṭha Up. 2.2.7 — ‘some enter a womb, others a stationary thing, according to their deeds and knowledge.’ Meaning: species, lifespan and experience are karma’s three harvests.
2.14: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 44 again — dharma rises, adharma falls. Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 4.4.5 ‘good by good action’. Meaning: Yoga, Sāṃkhya and Upaniṣad agree that joy and pain are not random; they are returns on what was done.
2.15: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: this is SK 1’s opening, sharpened — even pleasure carries change, anxiety and conditioning, so ‘all is suffering’ for the discerning. SK 12 says the guṇas are pleasure, pain and delusion, always mixed. Veda: Chāndogya Up. 7.23.1 — ‘there is no happiness in the small; the infinite (bhūman) alone is happiness.’ Meaning: the point is not pessimism but an honest audit.
2.16: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 1–2 — remedies are sought for suffering that is ‘neither certain nor final’ under worldly means. Yoga narrows it: only future pain can be prevented. Veda: Muṇḍaka Up. 3.2.9 — ‘he crosses sorrow, crosses evil.’ Meaning: the past cannot be changed; the future still can.
2.17: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 21 — puruṣa and prakṛti join ‘like the lame and the blind’; this conjunction is the root cause. Veda: Ṛgveda 1.164.20, repeated in Muṇḍaka Up. 3.1.1 — ‘two birds, companions, on one tree: one eats the sweet fruit, the other looks on without eating.’ Meaning: the Veda’s oldest image of the seer and the seen.
2.18: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 12–13 almost word for word — the guṇas are for illumination (prakāśa), activity (pravṛtti) and restraint; prakṛti exists for experience and release (SK 56–58). Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 4.5 — the unborn she-goat, red, white and black, ‘bearing many offspring like herself’; Chāndogya Up. 6.4.1 gives the three colours as fire, water and food. Meaning: the Veda’s three colours become the three guṇas.
2.19: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: the four levels map SK 3 and 38 — specific (gross elements, senses), unspecific (tanmātras, ahaṃkāra), merely-marked (mahat) and unmarked (prakṛti). Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.3.10–11 — objects, mind, intellect, the great self, the unmanifest; Kaṭha 2.3.8 calls what is beyond ‘aliṅga’, unmarked — the same word. Meaning: the Kaṭha’s ladder is the oldest form of this map.
2.20: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 19 — puruṣa is ‘witness, isolated, neutral, seer, non-doer’. Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 3.7.23 — ‘the unseen seer, the unheard hearer … there is no other seer’; 4.3.15 — ‘this person is unattached (asaṅga).’ Meaning: the seer only appears to think, by lending its light to the mind.
2.21: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 17 — ‘because all compounds exist for another’; SK 56 — creation is for each puruṣa’s release. Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 2.4.5 — ‘not for love of the husband is the husband dear, but for love of the Self.’ Meaning: everything that is seen exists for the one who sees.
2.22: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 66 — ‘she has been seen by me,’ says one, and ceases; yet prakṛti goes on for others — implied by SK 18’s many puruṣas. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 4.5 — ‘one unborn lies with her, enjoying; another leaves her, having enjoyed.’ Meaning: the world ends for the freed, not for everyone.
2.23: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: owner and owned, SK 21’s pairing ‘for viewing and for release’. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 1.9 — ‘two unborn ones, the knower and the not-knower, the lord and the not-lord.’ Meaning: the meeting exists so each can be known for what it is.
2.24: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 44 — bondage from error; SK 63 — prakṛti binds herself by seven dispositions, all except knowledge. Veda: Muṇḍaka Up. 3.1.2 — the self ‘grieves, deluded by its helplessness (anīśā)’. Meaning: the cause of the knot is not-knowing, so its cure is knowing.
2.25: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 68 — ‘absolute and final isolation (kaivalya)’; Yoga uses the same word. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 6.11 — the Self is ‘witness, consciousness, alone (kevala), without guṇas.’ Meaning: ‘kaivalya’ comes from the Upaniṣad’s own word kevala.
2.26: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 37 — buddhi discerns the subtle difference between pradhāna and puruṣa; SK 64 — that knowledge, practised, becomes complete. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.2.1–2 — the wise ‘examine and distinguish (vivinakti)’ the good from the pleasant — the same root as viveka. Meaning: one steady distinction does what no ritual can.
2.27: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: the seven stages climb toward SK 64’s ‘I am not, nothing is mine, no I.’ Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 4.4.22 — ‘not this, not this (neti neti)’ — knowledge by stripping away. Meaning: insight matures by stages until nothing is left to know or do.
2.28: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 51 lists Sāṃkhya’s eight means (reasoning, instruction, study and the rest); Yoga’s eight limbs are the practice that ripens into SK 37’s discernment. Veda: Muṇḍaka Up. 3.1.8 — ‘by the grace of knowledge, the one pure in nature sees him’; Īśa Up. 15 asks the golden lid over truth to be removed. Meaning: practice removes impurity; light shows by itself.
2.29: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: Sāṃkhya has no stepwise method; Yoga supplies it. Veda: Maitrī Up. 6.18 gives a sixfold yoga — breath-control, withdrawal, meditation, concentration, reasoning (tarka) and samādhi. Patañjali adds yama, niyama and posture in front, drops tarka, and arrives at eight. Meaning: the eight limbs grow out of an older Vedic six.
2.30: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 2 faults Vedic ritual as ‘impure’ (aviśuddhi), which Vācaspati glosses as the harm in animal sacrifice. Ahiṃsā heads the list here for the same reason. Veda: Chāndogya Up. 3.17.4 lists austerity, giving, uprightness, non-harming (ahiṃsā) and truth as the true gifts of the inner sacrifice. Meaning: the ethics the Upaniṣads drew out of ritual become the first limb.
2.31: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: Sāṃkhya ethics is universal because puruṣas are alike in all bodies (SK 18–19). Veda: Īśa Up. 6–7 — ‘for one who sees oneness, what delusion, what sorrow?’ Meaning: a vow that knows no exceptions is a ‘great vow’.
2.32: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: purity and contentment build SK 23’s sattvic buddhi; study and surrender echo SK 51’s ‘study’ and Yoga’s Īśvara. Veda: Taittirīya Up. 1.11 — ‘speak truth, practise dharma, do not neglect study’; Śvetāśvatara Up. 6.18 — surrender to the Lord. Meaning: the niyamas are the Upaniṣad’s parting advice to the graduating student.
2.33: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: cultivating the opposite turns tamasic and rajasic buddhi toward sattva (SK 23). Veda: Śukla Yajurveda (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā) 34.1–6 — ‘may my mind be of auspicious resolve (śiva-saṅkalpa)’. Meaning: the Veda prays for a good mind; Yoga trains for one.
2.34: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: greed, anger and delusion map onto rajas, rajas-tamas and tamas (SK 12–13). Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 4.4.5 — what one does, causes, or wills, one becomes. Meaning: harm done, prompted or approved all return to the doer.
2.35: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: when buddhi is fully sattvic (SK 23), it no longer provokes the rajas in others. Veda: Īśa Up. 6 — one who sees the Self in all ‘has no aversion’; Taittirīya Up. 2.9 — ‘knowing the bliss of Brahman, one fears nothing.’ Meaning: the fearless cause no fear.
2.36: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: truth is a sattvic dharma of buddhi (SK 23). Veda: Muṇḍaka Up. 3.1.6 — ‘truth alone conquers (satyam eva jayate)’; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 1.4.14 equates truth with dharma. Meaning: words become effective when they are never false.
2.37: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: freedom from ‘mine’ is SK 64’s ‘nothing is mine’. Veda: Īśa Up. 1 — ‘enjoy by renouncing; do not covet anyone’s wealth (mā gṛdhaḥ kasya svid dhanam).’ Meaning: the one who does not grab finds things arrive.
2.38: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: conserved energy strengthens SK 23’s ‘power’ (aiśvarya). Veda: Muṇḍaka Up. 3.1.5 — the Self is gained by ‘constant brahmacarya’; Chāndogya Up. 8.5 calls brahmacarya the true sacrifice. Meaning: vigour is what is left when it is not spent.
2.39: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 64’s ‘nothing is mine’; SK 40 — the subtle body moves from life to life, which this insight sees. Veda: Īśa Up. 1 — ‘enjoy by renouncing’; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 4.4.3 — like a caterpillar crossing to the next blade of grass, the self moves on. Meaning: holding nothing, one sees how holding made the births.
2.40: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: seeing the body as gross element (SK 38–39) loosens ‘I am this body’. Veda: Chāndogya Up. 8.12.1 — ‘this body is mortal, held by death; it is the seat of the deathless, bodiless Self.’ Meaning: cleanliness becomes a lesson in what the body is.
2.41: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: ‘sattva-śuddhi’ — purification of buddhi — is the precondition SK 37 sets for discernment. Veda: Chāndogya Up. 7.26.2 — ‘when food is pure the sattva is pure; when the sattva is pure, memory is firm’; Muṇḍaka Up. 3.1.8 — ‘the one of purified sattva sees him.’ Meaning: the Upaniṣad’s exact phrase becomes a stage of practice.
2.42: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: a notable difference — SK 50 lists nine ‘contentments’ (tuṣṭi) as obstacles, because they stop the search too early. Yoga praises contentment as unsurpassed happiness. The two meet if Yoga’s santoṣa is contentment with what one has, not with what one has understood. Veda: Chāndogya Up. 7.23 — ‘the infinite alone is happiness.’ Meaning: be content with your lot, never with your ignorance.
2.43: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: tapas burns impurity in the instruments (SK 32: the thirteen organs). Veda: Taittirīya Up. 3.2 — ‘seek to know Brahman by tapas; tapas is Brahman’; Śvetāśvatara Up. 2.12 — ‘no sickness, no ageing, no death for one who has gained a body made of the fire of yoga.’ Meaning: discipline refines the body and senses into fit instruments.
2.44: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 51 lists study (adhyayana) among Sāṃkhya’s eight perfections. Veda: Taittirīya Up. 1.9 — ‘study and teaching’ follow every virtue; Kaṭha Up. 1.2.23 — the Self ‘reveals its own form’ to the one it chooses. Meaning: recitation and study open a two-way door.
2.45: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: Īśvara is Yoga’s addition to Sāṃkhya (see 1.23). Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 6.23 — ‘to the great-souled one who has highest devotion to God, and to the teacher as to God, these truths shine.’ Meaning: surrender is a short road, because it removes the one who blocks the way.
2.46: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: posture steadies the gross body (SK 39) so the subtle can be worked on. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 2.8 — ‘holding the body steady, with the three upper parts erect’; 2.10 — in a clean, level place, free of pebbles, fire and sand, pleasing to the mind. Meaning: the Upaniṣad already gives the seat; Patañjali gives its two qualities.
2.47: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: relaxing effort lets rajas settle (SK 13: rajas is restless). Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 2.15 — seeing the truth of Brahman ‘with the Self as a lamp’; Kaṭha Up. 1.2.20 — the Self ‘greater than the great’, the infinite one rests in. Meaning: posture completes itself when the body forgets to try.
2.48: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: pleasure and pain are guṇa pairs (SK 12); a steady body stops reacting to them. Veda: Chāndogya Up. 8.12.1 — ‘pleasure and pain do not touch the bodiless’; Gītā 2.14 — ‘heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go — endure them.’ Meaning: steadiness in the body is the first taste of the Self’s untouched state.
2.49: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 29 — the five breaths are the shared function of buddhi, ahaṃkāra and manas, so steadying breath steadies all three. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 2.9 — ‘restraining the breaths here … one should hold the mind like a chariot yoked to wild horses’; Atharvaveda 11.4.1 — ‘homage to Prāṇa, in whose control is all this.’ Meaning: breath is the rein of the mind.
2.50: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: careful measurement mirrors Sāṃkhya’s habit of counting (SK 3, 22). Veda: Chāndogya Up. 5.19–23 offers the meal to the five breaths in turn — a ritual already focused on prāṇa. Meaning: the Vedic attention to breath becomes a measured practice.
2.51: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: the fourth goes beyond in- and out-breath, as SK 65’s puruṣa goes beyond prakṛti’s movement. Veda: Māṇḍūkya Up. 7 — the fourth (caturtha), beyond waking, dream and sleep. Meaning: Yoga borrows the Upaniṣad’s idea of a ‘fourth’ that is not another of the three.
2.52: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: the covering is tamas over sattva’s light (SK 13). Veda: Īśa Up. 15 — ‘the face of truth is covered by a golden lid; remove it, O Pūṣan.’ Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 1.3.28 — ‘from darkness lead me to light.’ Meaning: breath-practice answers the Upaniṣad’s prayer.
2.53: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: manas becomes fit for steady attention (SK 27: manas deliberates). Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.3.6 — ‘for one with understanding and a mind always yoked, the senses obey like good horses.’ Meaning: the horses are now ready to be driven.
2.54: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 26–28 — the senses only present objects to the inner organ; withdrawn, they follow it inward. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.3.3–4 — the body a chariot, intellect the driver, mind the reins, senses the horses; Kaṭha 2.1.1 — the senses were pierced outward. Gītā 2.58 — like a tortoise drawing in its limbs. Meaning: the horses come home with the driver.
2.55: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: full mastery of the eleven senses of SK 26–27. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.3.5–6 — for the undiscerning the senses run like wild horses; for the discerning they obey. Meaning: the outer limbs end where the Kaṭha’s chariot is finally under control.
